learn.b: Kotlin programs start running in a function called main. Inside it, println prints a line of text. Text goes inside double quotes.
The keyword fun declares a function. The body goes between curly braces. Kotlin does not need semicolons at the end of lines, and indentation is just for readability.
println prints the text and then moves to a new line. print prints the text and stays on the same line, so the next output continues right after it.
A comment is a note for humans that the computer ignores. Use // for one line and /* ... */ for several lines. Kotlin runs on the JVM and its files end in .kt.

learn.b: Use val for a value that never changes (read-only) and var for a variable that can change. Prefer val when you can.
learn.code:
val name = "Kai"
var score = 0
score = 10

learn.b: Kotlin guesses the type from the value, so you rarely write it. You can also write the type after a colon: val age: Int = 14.
learn.code:

val b: Double = 2.5
val c = true       // Boolean

learn.b: Int holds whole numbers, Long holds big whole numbers (write 5L), Double holds decimals, Float needs an f (1.5f), Boolean is true or false, Char is one character in single quotes, and String is text.
learn.code:

val letter = 'K'

learn.b: The operators are + - * / and % (remainder). Dividing two Ints gives an Int, so 7 / 2 is 3. Types do not convert by themselves: use toDouble(), toInt() and so on.
learn.code:

println(7 / 2.0)
println(7 % 2)
println(3.9.toInt())

learn.b: A String is text in double quotes. Use + to join strings, length to count characters, and indexes like s[0] to get a character (counting from 0).

learn.b: if runs code when a condition is true. Comparison operators are == != < > <= >=, and you combine conditions with && (and), || (or) and ! (not). Use else if for more branches.
In Kotlin, if gives back a value, so you can assign it. This replaces the ternary operator from other languages. When used this way, else is required.
learn.code:
val a = 4
val b = 9
val max = if (a > b) a else b
println(max)

learn.b: when is Kotlin's powerful switch. It checks a value against branches in order and runs the first match. No break is needed, and else covers everything left.
when can also return a value, and branches can use ranges with in or types with is. Without an argument it works like an if-else chain.
learn.code:
val n = 15
val size = when {
    n < 10 -> "small"
    n in 10..20 -> "medium"
    else -> "large"
}
println(size)

A for loop goes through anything you can iterate, such as a range or a list. The variable is created for you, with no var needed.
while repeats as long as its condition is true, checking first. do-while runs the body once before it checks.
break leaves the loop at once. continue skips to the next round. To check membership use in, like if (x in 1..10).

learn.b: Write fun, a name, parameters with types, then the return type after a colon. Use return to send back a value. Functions with no useful result return Unit, which you can leave out.
If a function is just one expression, use = instead of braces and return. Kotlin infers the return type.
learn.code:
fun square(x: Int) = x * x
println(square(4))

learn.b: Give a parameter a default value with = and callers can leave it out. This replaces many overloads from other languages.
You can pass arguments by name, in any order, which makes calls easier to read and lets you skip defaults in the middle.
learn.code:
fun box(w: Int = 1, h: Int = 1) = w * h
println(box(h = 5))
println(box(w = 2, h = 3))

learn.b: In Kotlin a normal type like String can never hold null, so the compiler stops many crashes before they happen. Writing val s: String = null is an error.
learn.code:
val s: String = "hi"
// val t: String = null   // error

learn.b: Add a question mark to allow null: String?. Before using it you must handle the null case.
learn.code:
var name: String? = "Ana"
name = null
println(name)

learn.b: The safe call ?. runs only if the value is not null, otherwise gives null. The Elvis operator ?: gives a default when the left side is null.
learn.code:
val s: String? = null
println(s?.length)
println(s?.length ?: 0)

learn.b: You can test with if (s != null) and Kotlin then treats s as non-null. The operator !! says trust me and crashes if it is null, so avoid it. The let function runs code only when not null.

qs.why: a ?: b means a if not null, else b.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: s is null so s?.length is null and Elvis gives 0.

qs.q: The !! operator is the safest way to handle null.
qs.why: It throws an exception if the value is null.

learn.b: listOf makes a read-only list, setOf a set with no duplicates, and mapOf pairs keys to values using to. Use mutableListOf and similar when you want to add or remove items.
learn.code:
val nums = listOf(1, 2, 3)
val m = mapOf("a" to 1, "b" to 2)
val items = mutableListOf("x")
items.add("y")
println(nums[0])
println(m["b"])

learn.b: Collections have size, and you can loop with for. Use in to test membership and indexes like list[0] to read items.
learn.code:

println(fruit.size)
for (f in fruit) println(f)
println("pear" in fruit)

learn.b: A lambda is a small function written in braces: { x -> x * 2 }. If it has one parameter you can refer to it as it. When a lambda is the last argument it can go outside the parentheses.
learn.code:

println(double(4))
val list = listOf(1, 2, 3)
println(list.map { it * 10 })

learn.b: map changes every item, filter keeps items that pass a test, and sum, count, first and sorted work on lists. They return new collections.
learn.code:
val n = listOf(1, 2, 3, 4)
println(n.filter { it % 2 == 0 })
println(n.map { it * it })
println(n.sum())

learn.b: A class describes a kind of thing. The primary constructor sits in the header, and val or var turns a parameter into a property. Create an object by calling the class like a function, with no new keyword.
An init block runs when an object is created. Functions inside a class are called methods, and you reach members with a dot. Inside the class, this means the current object.
Mark a class data when it mainly holds values. Kotlin generates toString, equals, copy and component functions for you.
learn.code:
data class User(val name: String, val age: Int)
val u = User("Ana", 12)
println(u)
val v = u.copy(age = 13)
println(u == User("Ana", 12))

learn.b: Kotlin classes are final by default. Mark a class open to allow subclasses, write the parent after a colon, and mark overridable members open too. Use override in the child.

An interface lists functions a class promises to have and can include default code. A class can implement many interfaces. An abstract class cannot be created directly and can leave functions without a body.
A coroutine is a light task that can pause without blocking a thread. You need the kotlinx.coroutines library. launch starts one, delay pauses it, and runBlocking waits for them in main.
A suspend function can pause a coroutine, and can only be called from another suspend function or a coroutine. async starts work and returns a result you collect with await.
